Banished to a remote province after his wife's affair with Nero, this Roman noble later murdered his ally Galba to seize the throne, becoming the second ruler of the Year of the Four Emperors — who was he?
First featured in a late-12th-century tale by Chrétien de Troyes, this Knight of the Round Table was the original hero of the Grail quest before later authors replaced him with Galahad — who is he?
Perceval: One of King Arthur's legendary Knights.
Known as the 'earth shaker' in Bronze Age cult, this Greek god of the sea and horses could strike his trident to create springs — who is he?
Poseidon: Ancient Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses.
Before serving as Chicago's mayor and later as U.S. ambassador to Japan, this Illinois Democrat was Barack Obama's first White House chief of staff — who is he?
Rahm Emanuel: American politician and diplomat (born 1959)

This American naval aviator and polar explorer discovered Mount Sidley — Antarctica's largest dormant volcano — and claimed to be first to reach both Poles by air, though the North Pole claim remains disputed. Who was he?
Richard E. Byrd: American naval officer (1888–1957)
This August 1992 siege in Boundary County, Idaho began when U.S. Marshals came to arrest Randy Weaver — over a sawed-off shotgun sale — after he was given the wrong court date. What event was it?
Ruby Ridge standoff: 1992 siege and shootout in Idaho, US.

In July 1984, a lone gunman killed 22 people at a fast-food restaurant in a Southern California border town before a police sniper ended his 77-minute rampage — for years it held the record as the deadliest such attack by a single gunman in U.S. history. What is this event known as?
San Ysidro McDonald's massacre: 1984 mass shooting in California, U.S.

Entering a power-sharing arrangement with his father in 2022, this politician became president after winning 73% of the vote in what's widely considered a sham election, making his nation the first in modern Central Asia ruled by a father-son dynasty — who is he?
Serdar Berdimuhamedow: President of Turkmenistan since 2022.

In 1793, Royalist rebels in this vital French naval port — home to a third of the French fleet — invited a 13,000-strong Anglo-Spanish force to help hold the city against advancing Republican troops — what military engagement was this?
Siege of Toulon (1793): Part of the War of the First Coalition.
This Italian entrepreneur-turned-politician founded a university in 2006, has presided over a football club since 2017, and became mayor of an Umbrian city in 2023 — who is he?
Stefano Bandecchi: Italian politician and entrepreneur. Stefano Bandecchi (born 4 April 1961) is an Italian politician and entrepreneur.
Reigning over the Georgian Golden Age from 1184 to 1213, this Bagrationi monarch was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right and was given the title 'King' in medieval sources — who was she?
Tamar I: Queen of Georgia from 1184 to 1213. Tamar was successful in neutralizing this opposition and embarked on an energetic foreign policy aided by the decline of the hostile Seljuk Turks.

This South Australian premier governed for over 26 years — the longest unbroken stretch of any elected leader in Australian history — and was famous for shamelessly haranguing federal leaders into funding his state. Who was he?
Thomas Playford IV: 20th-century Australian politician and fruit grower (1896–1981)
Dubbed 'the Nelson of the East' by Western reporters, this Imperial Japanese Navy admiral penned Russia's fleet into Port Arthur before a decisive 1905 victory at Tsushima — who is he?

Raiding, trading, and settling from Scandinavia across Europe, North Africa, and even Newfoundland between the late 8th and 11th centuries, this seafaring people helped establish Kievan Rus'. Who were they?
Vikings: Norse seafarers, merchants and raiders.

The first conflict of the Napoleonic Wars, this 1805–1806 struggle pitted Napoleon's France against an alliance of Britain, Austria, Russia, Naples, Sicily, and Sweden, and included the Battle of Trafalgar — which conflict?
War of the Third Coalition: 1805–1806 conflict during the Napoleonic Wars. The Royal Navy, however, assured its naval dominance at the Battle of Trafalgar in October 1805.

This Polish resistance leader deliberately got himself captured by the Germans in 1940 so he could infiltrate a notorious concentration camp and organize a resistance movement from within — who is he?
Serving as Japan's foreign minister from 2023 to 2024, she previously held the justice portfolio and worked on gender-equality policy under two different prime ministers — who is she?
Which of these people was born first?
Kitty Oppenheimer (born 1910) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four.
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Pope Sylvester II is an astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Eric Weinstein is a mathematician. Eric Ross Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.
What is the atomic number of Radium?
Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
What is the atomic number of Zinc?
Zinc is a chemical element; it has symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
In what year was David Baszucki born?
David Baszucki: David Brent Baszucki (buh-ZOO-ki; born January 20, 1963) is a Canadian-born American entrepreneur, engineer, and software developer.
In what year was Arthur C. Clarke born?
Arthur C. Clarke: Clarke was a science fiction writer, an avid populariser of space travel, and a futurist of distinguished ability.
In what year was Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz born?
Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz: Leibniz, along with René Descartes and Baruch Spinoza, was one of the three influential early modern rationalists.
In what year did Bertrand Russell die?
Bertrand Russell: Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl Russell (18 May 1872 – 2 February 1970), was an English philosopher, logician, mathematician, and public intellectual.
In what year did Johannes Kepler die?
Johannes Kepler (27 December 1571 – 15 November 1630) was a German polymath who was an astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, natural philosopher and music theorist.
In what year was Eris discovered?
Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Metronidazole: Pfizer. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Gurjar: India. The Gurjar are an agricultural ethnic community, residing mainly in India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan, divided internally into various clan groups.
Who is credited with discovering Zirconium?
Zirconium: Martin Heinrich Klaproth. Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
Who is credited with discovering Quetzalcoatlus?
Quetzalcoatlus: Douglas A. Lawson. Quetzalcoatlus is a genus of azhdarchid pterosaur that lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in North America.
Who is credited with discovering Silicon carbide?
Silicon carbide: Edward Goodrich Acheson. Silicon carbide (SiC), also known as carborundum, is a hard chemical compound of silicon and carbon.
Who is credited with discovering Bromine?
Bromine: Carl Jacob Löwig. Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.
An economist who once worked for the IMF and later served as Prime Minister of Côte d'Ivoire from 1990 to 1993, this politician has been the country's president since 2010 — name this leader?
Alassane Ouattara (French; born 1 January 1942) is an Ivorian politician and economist who has been President of Ivory Coast (Cte d'Ivoire) since 2010.
This English number theorist became a mathematical legend by proving Fermat's Last Theorem, earning the 2016 Abel Prize and a knighthood. Who is he?
Andrew Wiles (born 11 April 1953) is an English mathematician and a Royal Society Research Professor at the University of Oxford, specialising in number theory.
Which noble gas, symbol Ar and atomic number 18, is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere — more plentiful there than carbon dioxide or neon?
Argon is a chemical element; it has symbol Ar and atomic number 18.
The only mammals capable of true sustained flight, members of this order — the second largest among mammals — fly using long digits webbed by a thin membrane. What are they?
Bat (order Chiroptera) are winged mammals, the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight.
Native to India and Nepal, this medium-sized antelope sports a striking two-tone coat, with males growing corkscrew horns up to 75 cm long. Which animal is it?
Blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra), also known as the Indian antelope, is a medium-sized antelope native to India and Nepal.
An Austrian-born psychologist who directed Chicago's Orthogenic School, he was an early and controversial writer on autism whose ideas grew out of Freud — who was he?

Bruno Bettelheim (August 28, 1903 - March 13, 1990) was an Austrian-born American psychologist, scholar, public intellectual and writer who spent most of his academic and clinical career in the United States.

This group of diseases directly affecting the heart muscle itself may show few symptoms early on but can progress to heart failure, irregular heartbeat, and an increased risk of sudden cardiac death — what condition is it?
Cardiomyopathy is a group of primary diseases of the heart muscle. In dilated cardiomyopathy the ventricles enlarge and weaken.

Used to disinfect skin before surgery, sterilize surgical tools, treat oral yeast infections, and keep urinary catheters clear, this antiseptic compound comes as a gluconate or acetate salt — what is it?
Chlorhexidine is a disinfectant and antiseptic which is used for skin disinfection before surgery and to disinfect surgical instruments.

With just two living species — the Sunda and Philippine varieties — these Southeast Asian gliders are arboreal primatomorphs more closely related to primates than to any other animal — what is this group called?
Colugo are arboreal gliding primatomorphs that are native to Southeast Asia.
Usually viral and often worse at night, this childhood respiratory infection swells the windpipe to produce a barking, brassy cough and noisy breathing — what's the condition?
This annual herb in the celery family, native to North Africa and West Asia, is grown across Eurasia for both its feathery leaves and its seeds, both used to flavor food — what herb is it?
Dill (Anethum graveolens) is an annual herb in the celery family Apiaceae.
Sometimes occurring spontaneously during sleep as a nocturnal emission, this process involves the discharge of semen through the urethra — what is it called?
Ejaculation is the discharge of semen (the ejaculate; normally containing sperm) from the penis through the urethra.

Combining lab and field science with strong ties to ecology and evolutionary biology, this discipline earned three of its founders a shared 1973 Nobel Prize for their work on animal behavior — what field is it?
Ethology is a branch of zoology that studies the behaviour of non-human animals.
The lightest halogen, this pale yellow gas is so reactive it combines with nearly every other element except the light noble gases. What element is it (symbol F)?
Fluorine is a chemical element; it has the symbol F and atomic number 9.

The first person in Germany to hold a professorship dedicated to experimental physics, he is remembered for his posthumous 'waste book' notebooks and for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him. Who is he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg (1 July 1742 - 24 February 1799) was a German physicist, satirist, and Anglophile.
Endemic to Africa and among the oldest of the gallinaceous birds, this family branched off before New World quail evolutionarily — name the birds?
Guinea fowl are birds of the family Numididae in the order Galliformes.
Planted for land reclamation thanks to its nitrogen-fixing, erosion-resisting root system, this deciduous shrub genus's berries also show up in human and animal food products — what genus is it?
Hippophae is a genus of flowering plants in the family Elaeagnaceae.
Prized in folk medicine as an antiseptic and expectorant, this Lamiaceae shrub grows wild from Southern Europe to the Caspian Sea area — which plant is it?
Hyssopus officinalis is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
A Scottish surgeon who corrected clubfoot and squints, he's also dubbed by some the 'Father of Modern Hypnotism' — pioneering both hypnotic and chemical anaesthesia. Who was this gentleman scientist?
James Braid (surgeon) (19 June 1795 - 25 March 1860) was a Scottish surgeon, natural philosopher, and "gentleman scientist".
Honored across Asia as a model healer and "Medicine King," this 5th-century BCE physician of Rajgir tended to King Bimbisāra — and to the Buddha himself. Who was he?
Jīvaka was the personal physician of the Buddha and the Indian King Bimbisra.
Also known as Al-Kashi's theorem, which trigonometry rule relates the lengths of a triangle's three sides to the cosine of one of its angles?

Law of cosines (also known as the cosine formula or cosine rule or Al-Kashi's theorem) relates the lengths of the sides of a triangle to the cosine of one of its angles. The law of cosines is useful for solving a triangle when all three sides or two sides and their included angle are given.
Descended from the YF-22 prototype, this supersonic air-superiority stealth fighter saw Boeing build its wings and aft fuselage while the prime contractor handled final assembly — what is it?
Lockheed Martin F-22 Raptor is an American twin-engine, jet-powered, all-weather, supersonic stealth fighter aircraft.

This psychiatric state of abnormally elevated energy and mood is sometimes called the mirror image of depression, though its heightened feelings can turn irritable or anxious just as easily as euphoric — what is it called?
Mania (also known as manic syndrome) is a psychiatric behavioral syndrome defined as a state of abnormally elevated arousal, affect, and energy level.
Named in 1925 as an abbreviation of its chemical structure, this essential amino acid is required to kick-start protein synthesis — which amino acid is this?
Methionine (symbol Met or M) is an essential amino acid in humans.

Sharing the insect order Lepidoptera with butterflies but typically sporting duller, darker wing patterns, this group includes roughly 160,000 mostly nocturnal species, many still undescribed by science — name this group of insects?
Moth are a group of winged insect of the order Lepidoptera, the other well-known members of which are butterflies, they are characterized by dark or dull patterned wings.

This Renaissance polymath put the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the universe in a 1543 book published just before his death — likely arriving independently at an idea Aristarchus of Samos had floated eighteen centuries earlier. Who is he?
Nicolaus Copernicus (19 February 1473 - 24 May 1543) was a Renaissance polymath who formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center.

These pouched mammals originated in South America and crossed into the north during the Great American Interchange; one species is so common in the U.S. that people just call it a 'possum.' What is it?
Opossum are members of the marsupial order Didelphimorphia endemic to the Americas.
This British theoretical physicist, one of the founders of quantum mechanics, coined the term 'quantum electrodynamics' and shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Erwin Schrödinger — who is he?
Paul Dirac (dih-RAK; 8 August 1902 - 20 October 1984) was a British theoretical physicist who is considered to be one of the founders of quantum mechanics.
This genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae is found mainly in northern South America, with a single species ranging into Central America — name this genus?
Phoneutria is a genus of spiders in the family Ctenidae.
Born Joseph Ratzinger in Bavaria, this pontiff led the Catholic Church from 2005 until an unusual resignation in 2013, after which he adopted an 'emeritus' title — who was he?
Pope Benedict XVI (born Joseph Alois Ratzinger; 16 April 1927 - 31 December 2022) was the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 2005 until his resignation in 2013.
Nesting in burrows or rock crevices on coastal cliffs, this black-and-white seabird can dive underwater to feed and beats its short wings up to 400 times per minute in flight — what bird is it?
Puffin are any of three species of small alcids (auks) in the bird genus Fratercula.

Covering more than 100 conditions like lupus and Sjögren's syndrome and overlapping heavily with immunology, this branch of medicine tackles inflammation in the joints, muscles and bones — what is it called?

Rheumatology (from Ancient Greek (rhema) 'flowing current') is a branch of medicine devoted to the diagnosis and management of disorders of which the common feature is inflammation in the bones, muscles, joints, and internal organs.
This American painter turned inventor co-developed a telegraph system and became the namesake of the dot-dash code that helped make telegraphy commercially viable — who is he?
Samuel Morse (April 27, 1791 - April 2, 1872) was an American inventor and painter.
The smallest of Japan's six native dog breeds, this small, alert hunting dog's name literally translates to 'brushwood dog,' reflecting its original job of flushing game — which breed?
Shiba Inu (Japanese) is a breed of hunting dog from Japan.

Extending from the base of the brainstem down to the lower back, this tubular bundle of nervous tissue is covered by the meninges and, together with the brain, makes up the central nervous system — name this structure?

Spinal cord is a long, thin, tubular structure made up of nervous tissue that extends from the medulla oblongata in the lower brainstem to the lumbar region of the vertebral column (backbone) of vertebrate animals.
Time named this marine biologist its first "Hero for the Planet" in 1998, the same year she became a National Geographic Explorer — and she was also NOAA's first chief scientist. Who is she?
Sylvia Earle (born August 30, 1935) is an American marine biologist, oceanographer, explorer, writer, and lecturer.
Raised by a wealthy uncle after his father fled following a fight, this English philosopher laid out an influential social contract theory in his 1651 book 'Leviathan' — who is he?

Thomas Hobbes (HOBZ; 5 April 1588 - 4 December 1679) was an English philosopher and political theorist, best known for his 1651 book Leviathan, in which he expounds an influential formulation of social contract theory.
First isolated as a metal in 1783, this element is drawn from ores like scheelite and wolframite — the latter lending it an alternative name. Which metal is it?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from) and atomic number 74.

This forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth can result from food poisoning, pregnancy, motion sickness, or more serious causes like brain tumors, and is usually preceded by nausea — name this bodily reaction?
Vomiting (scientifically known as emesis, and otherwise known as puking, and throwing up) is the forceful expulsion of the contents of one's stomach through the mouth and sometimes the nose.
Twice Egypt's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, this archaeologist has dug across the Nile Delta, the Western Desert, and the Upper Nile Valley — who is he?
Zahi Hawass (born May 28, 1947) is an Egyptian archaeologist, Egyptologist, and former Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, a position he held twice.
Widespread across Europe and into East Asia, this venomous snake looms large in British folklore but rarely delivers a fatal bite — what reptile?
Adder: Species of venomous snake. Vipera berus, commonly known as the common European adder and the common European viper, is a species of venomous snake in the family Viperidae.
This Italian physicist built the first true electric battery in 1799 and discovered methane, disproving the idea that electricity could only come from living bodies — who is he?
Alessandro Volta: Italian chemist and physicist (1745–1827)
Formed naturally around volcanic vents and on burning coal dumps, this white crystalline salt is mildly acidic in solution and is used as both a fertilizer and food additive — which compound?
Ammonium chloride: Chemical compound. Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as [NH4]Cl.
This scientific practice of systematically measuring the human body has been used in paleoanthropology, historical living-standards research, and modern clothing design — what is it called?
Anthropometry: Measurement of the human individual.
Literally meaning "hardening of the arteries," this umbrella term covers vascular disorders marked by abnormal thickening and loss of elasticity in artery walls — what is it called?
Arteriosclerosis: Thickening, hardening and loss of elasticity of the walls of arteries.
Sharing the 2015 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Tomas Lindahl and Paul Modrich, this Turkish-American scientist was honored for mechanistic studies of DNA repair — who is he?
Aziz Sancar: Turkish biochemist and molecular biologist (born 1946)
A likely hybrid of lemon and a bitter citrus relative, this fragrant fruit flavors tea, snus, and perfume, though it can heighten skin's sensitivity to sunlight — which fruit?
Credited with kicking off the Jet Age, this swept-wing quadjet airliner entered regular passenger service with Pan Am in October 1958 — which aircraft?

Best known for his role as Ben Hunter in a soapy prime-time revenge drama, this American actor also starred as Will Davis on The CW's 'Privileged' and Kyle Parks on Lifetime's 'The Client List.' Who is he?
Formed when quicklime reacts with water, this compound goes by names like slaked lime and builders' lime, and is used in food prep under the additive code E526 — what is it?
Calcium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Ca(OH)2.

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like herb is brewed into calming teas and can trigger uterine contractions in its Roman variety — what is it?
Chamomile: Common name for several daisy-like plants.
In this chronic liver condition, healthy tissue is replaced by scar tissue and regenerative nodules, choking blood flow and causing portal hypertension — what is it called?
Cirrhosis: Chronic disease of the liver, characterized by fibrosis.

Nicknamed 'flying lemurs' despite not being lemurs at all, these Southeast Asian gliding mammals are primates' closest living relatives and belong to an order whose name means 'skin wing' — what are they called?
Its round nuts distinguish it from the longer filbert, and its coppiced wood once built wattle-and-daub walls across England — which shrub?
Corylus avellana: Species of tree (common hazel)
Two polynucleotide chains coil around each other into a double helix to carry the genetic instructions of nearly every living thing — what is this macromolecule?
DNA: Molecule that carries genetic information.
Sold under the brand name Valium, this benzodiazepine anxiolytic treats anxiety, seizures, alcohol withdrawal, and muscle spasms — and can even induce memory loss during procedures; what is it?
Diazepam: Benzodiazepine sedative. Diazepam, sold under the brand name Valium among others, is a medication of the benzodiazepine family that acts as an anxiolytic.
The only living relative of the extinct Steller's sea cow, this seagrass-grazing marine mammal is most abundant in the waters of northern Australia — what is it?
Dugong: Species of marine mammal. It is one of four living species of the order Sirenia, which also includes three species of manatees.
Co-founding Mattel with his wife Ruth, this inventor helped bring Barbie, Hot Wheels, and Chatty Cathy to toy shelves — who is he?
Elliot Handler: American inventor and business magnate (1916–2011)
Made by yeast fermenting sugars and once used as a general anesthetic, this colorless flammable liquid is the world's second most consumed drug, behind only caffeine — what is it?
Known for its smooth silvery-grey bark and toxin-laced but edible nuts, this deciduous tree native to Europe includes the striking copper-leaved cultivar among its ornamentals — which species?
Fagus sylvatica: Species of deciduous tree. It is native to much of Europe, growing in humid climates.
This normal, occasionally embarrassing bodily process brings intestinal gas to the rectum, pressurizes it with muscle contractions, and releases it through the anus — what is it?
Flatulence: Bodily function of expelling intestinal gas from the anus.
Known as the brain's chief inhibitory neurotransmitter, this compound is also sold as a dietary supplement despite debate over whether it crosses the blood-brain barrier — what is it?
GABA: Main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the mammalian brain.
Caught from contaminated water and common among travelers and children, this parasitic infection causes fatty, sticky diarrhea weeks after exposure — what is it?
Giardiasis: Parasitic disease that results in diarrhea.
With a black head, white cheeks and yellow underparts, this widespread European songbird was split from two Asian relatives after 2005 DNA studies?
Great tit: Passerine bird in the tit family Paridae.

Nicknamed the 'Halloween beetle' in North America for invading homes each October to overwinter, this extremely color-variable insect was introduced there from eastern Asia to control aphids — what species is it?
Harmonia axyridis: Species of beetle. Harmonia axyridis is a lady beetle or ladybird species that is most commonly known as the harlequin, Asian, or multicoloured Asian lady beetle.
Known scientifically as singultus, this involuntary diaphragm spasm closes the glottis in about 35 milliseconds to produce a signature sound — what reflex is it?
Hiccup: Involuntary contraction of the diaphragm. The rhythm of the hiccup, or the time between hiccups, tends to be relatively constant.

Made of one oxygen and one hydrogen atom bonded together with a negative charge, this ion is the active base in the sodium compound used to produce millions of tons of industrial chemicals yearly. What ion is it?
Patented in 1961 and used to fight fever, pain and inflammation by blocking the cyclooxygenase enzyme, this drug sits on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Before he proposed that the Earth behaves like one self-regulating living system, this English independent scientist built the detector that first revealed CFCs lurking in our atmosphere. Who was he?
A former Navy SEAL turned physician, this NASA astronaut flew to the International Space Station in 2025 as part of Expedition 72/73 after earning a Silver Star for valor in combat — who is he?
Jonny Kim: American astronaut, physician, and former U.S. Navy SEAL (born 1984)
This Gram-negative rod bacterium can turn deadly if aspirated into the lungs, producing a telltale bloody, brownish-yellow jelly-like sputum — which pathogen?
Klebsiella pneumoniae: Species of bacterium. Klebsiella pneumoniae is a Gram-negative, non-motile, encapsulated, lactose-fermenting, facultative anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
Named after the Latin for 'ghosts of the dead' for their large eyes and nocturnal habits, these primates are found only on Madagascar — what are they?
Lemur: Clade of primates endemic to the island of Madagascar.
Also called pseudocoma, this condition leaves a fully conscious patient paralyzed except for blinking and vertical eye movement, coined by two neurologists in 1966 — what is it called?
Locked-in syndrome: Condition in which a patient is aware but completely paralysed.
Nicknamed for a Native American tribe, this mulberry-family tree produces a bumpy, orange-like fruit that oozes sticky white latex and is rarely eaten by animals — what's its scientific name?
Maclura pomifera: Plant species in the fig family.
In 2014 this Stanford mathematician became the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal, honored for her work on the geometry of Riemann surfaces — who was she?
Patented in 1922 and later marketed as Novalgin or Analgin, this painkiller's sale is restricted in some countries due to a rare blood-cell risk called agranulocytosis — what is it?
Metamizole: Medication. Metamizole or dipyrone is a painkiller, spasm reliever, and fever reliever drug.

Prized for their fur and related to weasels and otters, these semiaquatic carnivores have established wild populations in Britain and Denmark after farm escapes and animal-rights releases — what are they?
Mink: Mammal in the family Mustelidae.
This contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease is best known for causing painful swelling of the glands beside the jaw — its hallmark symptom. What is it?
Mumps: Human disease caused by paramyxovirus.
Discovered in 1885 by Carl Auer von Welsbach, this rare-earth element tarnishes quickly in air and produces pink, purple, and yellow compounds when oxidized — which element, atomic number 60?
Neodymium: Chemical element with atomic number 60 (Nd)

A French apothecary and physician who studied at Avignon until the plague closed it, he's far better remembered for 942 cryptic quatrains said to foretell the future — by what Latinised name is he known?
Nostradamus: French apothecary, astrologer and seer (1503–1566)
Sold under the brand name Tamiflu, this oral antiviral is recommended for high-risk patients within 48 hours of their first flu symptoms. What drug is it?
Oseltamivir: Antiviral medication used against influenza.
Believed to have originated in Sardinia and first cultivated in Britain in 1548, which herb is often used simply as a garnish today?
Parsley: Species of flowering plant in the celery family Apiaceae cultivated as an herb.
Smaller than 3 millimetres and caused by leaking capillaries, these tiny red or purple skin spots can be forensically significant when found around the eyes or neck — what are they called?
Petechia: Small red or purple blemish on the skin, eyes, etc. due to rupture of capillaries.

The most economically important member of the bromeliad family, this South American fruit became a 17th-century European symbol of luxury — and forms when many small flowers fuse into one — what is it?
Pineapple: Species of flowering plant in the family Bromeliaceae.
This deliquescent white salt helps make Dutch-process cocoa, soap, and glass, and can also turn up leaking from old alkaline batteries — what compound?
Potassium carbonate: Chemical compound. It is a white salt, which is soluble in water and forms a strongly alkaline solution.

Marked by delusions, hallucinations and disorganized thinking, this state — not a diagnosis itself — often stems from schizophrenia, bipolar disorder or alcohol-related brain damage — what is it called?
Psychosis: Abnormal condition of the mind.
Also called broccoli rabe, this bitter, vitamin K-rich cruciferous vegetable is a Mediterranean cuisine staple with edible leaves, buds, and stems — what is it?
This blue supergiant in Orion, also known as Beta Orionis, outshines the Sun by up to 363,000 times and anchors a system of at least four stars — which star?
Rigel: Brightest star in the constellation Orion.
Named after the Latin word for willow tree, from which it was first derived, this plant hormone and aspirin precursor shows up in anti-acne cosmetics — what is it?
Salicylic acid: Chemical compound used in medicines and industry.
These marine algae include the kelps that shelter fisheries and are estimated to produce at least half of Earth's oxygen — what are they collectively called?
Seaweed: Macroscopic marine algae. Seaweed, or macroalgae, refers to thousands of species of macroscopic, multicellular, marine algae.

This Irish mathematician and physicist held Cambridge's Lucasian Professorship for an unmatched 54 years, leaving his name on equations of fluid mechanics and a theorem of vector calculus — who is it?
Sir George Stokes, 1st Baronet: British mathematician and physicist (1819–1903)
This family of roughly 1,450 moths flies so swiftly on narrow wings and streamlined bodies that some species hover at flowers and are routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what's its scientific name?
Sphingidae: Family of insects. The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.

Distinct from addiction, this biopsychological condition occurs when a person's body has adapted so much to a psychoactive drug that stopping triggers withdrawal, requiring continued use just to function — what is this condition called?
Substance dependence: Need for a drug, whose discontinuation results in withdrawal symptoms.
This genus of flowering plants, commonly called dandelions, thrives nearly worldwide in yards, gardens, and roadsides — which genus?
